title: Security in React — XSS, CSRF, and Secure Patterns

subChunks.title: Security in React — XSS, CSRF, and Secure Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: Frontend security is not the backend's responsibility. React's JSX escapes output by default, but there are well-known escape hatches. Tokens stored in localStorage are readable by any script on your domain. CSRF attacks abuse cookies. Content Security Policy can prevent entire categories of injection attacks. Security is a set of deliberate decisions — defaults protect you from some things; you have to make the right choices for the rest.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
XSS — Cross-Site Scripting

// React's JSX escapes output by default — this is SAFE:
const userInput = '<script>alert("xss")</script>';
return <p>{userInput}</p>;  // Renders as escaped text, not HTML

// dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses escaping — only use with sanitised HTML:
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';

// ❌ DANGEROUS — execute arbitrary scripts:
return <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: userContent }} />;

// ✅ SAFE — sanitise first:
const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(userContent, {
  ALLOWED_TAGS: ['b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'a'],
  ALLOWED_ATTR: ['href'],
});
return <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: clean }} />;

// ❌ DANGEROUS — href injection:
const userUrl = 'javascript:alert(1)';
return <a href={userUrl}>Click me</a>;  // Executes script!

// ✅ SAFE — validate URLs:
function SafeLink({ href, children }) {
  const isValidUrl = href.startsWith('https://') || href.startsWith('/');
  if (!isValidUrl) return <span>{children}</span>;
  return <a href={href}>{children}</a>;
}

Token storage

// ❌ localStorage — readable by ANY JS on your domain (XSS risk):
localStorage.setItem('auth-token', token);

// ✅ HttpOnly cookies — not readable by JS, server sets them:
// Server response: Set-Cookie: auth-token=xxx; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict
// The browser sends the cookie automatically; JS can't read it

// ✅ If you must use JS-accessible storage, use memory:
let authToken: string | null = null; // In-memory, lost on refresh — pair with refresh token flow

// Token refresh pattern:
async function refreshAccessToken() {
  // Refresh token in HttpOnly cookie, access token in memory:
  const res = await fetch('/api/auth/refresh', { credentials: 'include' });
  const { accessToken } = await res.json();
  authToken = accessToken; // Short-lived, in memory only
}

CSRF — Cross-Site Request Forgery

// CSRF attacks trick the browser into making authenticated requests to your API
// from a malicious third-party site (the browser sends cookies automatically)

// Protection 1: SameSite=Strict cookie attribute (modern browsers):
// Set-Cookie: session=xxx; SameSite=Strict
// Browser won't send cookie on cross-site requests

// Protection 2: CSRF token (for older browser support):
// Server sends a CSRF token in the page; client echoes it in a header:
const csrfToken = document.querySelector('meta[name="csrf-token"]')?.content;

fetch('/api/quests/accept', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'X-CSRF-Token': csrfToken,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  credentials: 'include',
  body: JSON.stringify({ questId }),
});

// Protection 3: Check Origin/Referer header server-side
// Malicious sites can't forge these headers

Content Security Policy

// CSP prevents inline scripts and restricts which sources can load scripts:
// In index.html <head>:
<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
  content="
    default-src 'self';
    script-src 'self' 'nonce-RANDOM_NONCE';
    style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
    img-src 'self' data: https://cdn.arcane.academy;
    connect-src 'self' https://api.arcane.academy;
    frame-ancestors 'none';
  "
/>

// Or via HTTP header (more secure than meta tag):
// Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; ...

// React + strict CSP: avoid eval() (used by some bundlers in dev mode)
// Vite development mode uses eval — use nonce-based CSP or disable in prod only

Dependency security

# Audit for known vulnerabilities:
npm audit
npm audit fix

# Add to CI — fail if high severity:
npm audit --audit-level=high

# Automated PRs for updates:
# Enable GitHub Dependabot in .github/dependabot.yml:
# version: 2
# updates:
#   - package-ecosystem: npm
#     directory: /
#     schedule: { interval: weekly }
#     open-pull-requests-limit: 10

Vex: "The most common React security mistake: storing JWT tokens in localStorage. Any XSS vulnerability — in your code, a dependency, a third-party widget — can steal the token and hijack the session. HttpOnly cookies aren't readable by JS at all. If you must use localStorage, accept the risk, minimise the token lifetime, and layer defences."

storyBeats.text: A guild member pastes their quest description into the editor. It contains a script tag. The application renders it with dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Every member who views that quest executes the injected code. Their auth tokens are exfiltrated. The breach took 30 seconds to set up.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: XSS is not about bad users — it's about unsanitised output. React escapes JSX by default. The escape hatches are dangerouslySetInnerHTML, href with javascript:, and eval(). Never use them with user-controlled content. DOMPurify sanitises HTML on the client. HttpOnly cookies ensure stolen tokens via XSS are impossible. Layer defences.

storyBeats.speaker: DOMPurify for safe rich text rendering

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Audit and fix security vulnerabilities:

  • Write a SafeLink component that validates href values to only allow https:// and / paths
  • Write a RichText component that uses DOMPurify to sanitise HTML before using dangerouslySetInnerHTML (mock DOMPurify for the sandbox)
  • Write a useSecureFetch hook that automatically includes a CSRF token header on all non-GET requests
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Security audit and hardening for the quest board: (1) Audit every use of dangerouslySetInnerHTML and add DOMPurify sanitisation with a strict ALLOWED_TAGS allowlist. (2) Audit all anchor/link hrefs for javascript: injection — implement a SafeLink component used everywhere. (3) Add a Content Security Policy meta tag that blocks inline scripts, restricts connect-src to your API domain, and prevents framing (frame-ancestors none). (4) Run npm audit and fix or document all high/critical vulnerabilities. (5) Move any JWTs from localStorage to memory (with an HttpOnly refresh cookie handling persistence). Document the security decisions in a SECURITY.md file.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain XSS — how does an attacker inject a script into your React application, and what are the three React-specific escape hatches that bypass JSX's automatic escaping? Explain why localStorage is considered less secure than HttpOnly cookies for storing auth tokens — what specific attack does HttpOnly prevent? Walk through the CSRF attack flow — how does SameSite=Strict prevent it without needing a CSRF token?

questions.prompt: A user reports that clicking 'View Profile' on a quest description navigates to an unexpected URL. The href was stored as user input. What is the vulnerability and fix?
options: Href injection — user-controlled href values can use the javascript: protocol to execute scripts. Fix: validate all user-provided hrefs to only allow https:// and / paths before rendering in an anchor tag.
This is a React Router bug — user-provided hrefs bypass the router
The vulnerability is in the CSS — href values are safe in React
Add rel='noopener noreferrer' to the anchor tag to prevent this
questions.answer: Href injection — user-controlled href values can use the javascript: protocol to execute scripts. Fix: validate all user-provided hrefs to only allow https:// and / paths before rendering in an anchor tag.
questions.explanation: React does NOT escape href values. A href='javascript:alert(1)' renders as a clickable link that executes JavaScript. Any user-controlled value used in href, src, action, or similar attributes needs explicit validation. A SafeLink component that checks href.startsWith('https://') || href.startsWith('/') and renders a plain span for anything else is a simple, effective defence. rel='noopener noreferrer' is about opener access, not script injection.

questions.prompt: Your application uses localStorage to store the auth JWT. An attacker finds an XSS vulnerability via a third-party npm package. What can they do, and how would HttpOnly cookies have helped?
options: The attacker can run document.cookie or localStorage.getItem to read the JWT and exfiltrate it to their server — with HttpOnly cookies, JavaScript cannot read the cookie at all, making token theft via XSS impossible
XSS can't access localStorage — it's protected by the Same-Origin Policy
HttpOnly cookies would prevent the XSS vulnerability from being exploited
The attacker can only read the JWT if they have physical access to the device
questions.answer: The attacker can run document.cookie or localStorage.getItem to read the JWT and exfiltrate it to their server — with HttpOnly cookies, JavaScript cannot read the cookie at all, making token theft via XSS impossible
questions.explanation: Any JavaScript running on your domain — including injected scripts via XSS — can access localStorage and non-HttpOnly cookies. A single compromised dependency in node_modules is enough. HttpOnly cookies are flagged by the browser as inaccessible to JavaScript: document.cookie won't show them, and they cannot be read by any script. The browser sends them automatically with requests (which is why CSRF protection is also needed), but XSS can never steal them.
